title: Symmetry and Biomorphic Forms Characterize Roberta Gentry's Sensual Paintings
description: Through brilliant oranges and moody shades of blue, Los Angeles-based artist Roberta Gentry renders vivid, balanced compositions that, as she says
body:
Through brilliant oranges and moody shades of blue, Los Angeles-based artist Roberta Gentry renders vivid, balanced compositions that, as she says, take the senses seriously. Gentry has long been interested in the relationship between the constructed and the natural, cultivating abstract, biomorphic forms scaffolded by tall columns. 
Gravitating toward symmetry and restricted palettes, Gentry paints rhythmic pieces that adhere to an underlying grid. Every painting is the result of multiple layers of thinned acrylic, which build into subtle gradients that dissipate across the canvas.
“The Rose Lattice” (2026), acrylic on canvas, 36 x 48 inches
The paintings shown here are part of that artist’s upcoming solo exhibition, Blood Orange. Lush with color and texture, Gentry’s pieces reference the 16th-century La Dame à la licorne tapestries, comprised of six fiber works featuring a blond, lavishly dressed noblewoman flanked by a unicorn on one side and a lion on the other. Each piece correlates with one of the five senses, with text on the sixth reading “À Mon Seul Désirm,” or “to my only desire.”
While Blood Orange references the tapestries’ bold color palettes, Gentry also renders various elements they depict. The velvet gown the noblewoman wears, a towering pipe organ, and the orange trees anchoring the backdrop become central forms. 
Although scholars interpret the tapestries as directly referencing the sense, others take a broader, more nuanced approached. The latter posit that the fiber works speak to how we gather knowledge and information about the world—particularly through the sixth, more mysterious piece related to emotion—and this is another place where Gentry’s interests align. She often considers “how we construct mythologies to interpret and explain our lived experiences,” that emerges on the canvas through a tension between the order of the grid and the roving, unpredictable nature of organic growth. 
Blood Orange runs through October 24 at Track 16’s East Hollywood location. Find more from the artist on Instagram.
“Two Tails” (2026), acrylic on canvas, 14 x 18 inches
“Nine Holly Berries” (2026), acrylic on canvas, 14 x 18 inches
“A Golden Collar” (2026), acrylic on canvas, 48 x 60 inches
“Velvet Shoulders” (2026), acrylic on canvas, 36 x 48 inches
“The Organist’s Arbor” (2026), acrylic on canvas, 48 x 60 inches
“Ten Oranges” (2026), acrylic on canvas, 18 x 14 inches
“Unicorn” (2026), acrylic on canvas, 36 x 28 inches

title: Sara Anstis' Soft Pastels Summon Mythology, Dreams, and the Renaissance
description: A figure appears to have been subsumed by a bookcase, and another is swathed in a green sleeping bag beneath a makeshift tent. Whether navigating
body:
A figure appears to have been subsumed by a bookcase, and another is swathed in a green sleeping bag beneath a makeshift tent. Whether navigating a bathtub fitted with oars or sleeping in a bed while stacked like pancakes, the figures in Sara Anstis’ atmospheric drawings are immersed in curious activities. Hints of mysterious narratives, nursery rhymes, art historical iconography, and ancient symbolism make their way into enchanting and peculiar tableaux.
Anstis conjures a timeless air in the small-scale works of her solo show Pastels at Olney Gleason. Over the past couple of years, her palette has shifted to more muted, autumnal tones in contrast to her earlier works that featured vibrant, saturated hues and an almost glowing, neon quality. Recently, she’s looked to art history, particularly medieval and early Renaissance works.
“Ermine” (2026), pastel on paper, 13 3/8 x 18 1/8 inches
The stoic, three-quarter profiles of figure in “The Horse Rider,” for example, reflects expressions seen in the 15th-century work of the likes of Fra Angelico and Hans Memling. “The Painter” ties in the medieval art tradition of placing saints at the foot of a holy figure, this time depicted as women peering reverently not only toward a female artist but the empowering drawn likeness of a woman’s form.
Another recurring animal motif we closely associate with Leonardo da Vinci and his masterpiece “Lady with an Ermine.” For Anstis, these tributes are small in scale but rich in the recognition of women with a variety of talents and interests, not the least of which include motherhood.
The maternal theme emerges in works throughout the exhibition, influenced partly by German artist Paula Modersohn-Becker’s 1906 painting “Self-Portrait at 6th Wedding Anniversary.” Soft pastels are a symbolic and practical medium, building compositions that explore the fuzziness of dreams and the blurred edges of folk stories. “Three heads in a bed,” for example, brings to mind the nursery rhyme “Ten in the Bed,” which is sometimes sung as “Three in the Bed.” 
Long interested in mythology and subjectivity, Anstis renders figures and symbolic objects amid surreal settings. Some works adhere more closely to the conventions of portraiture while others reveal an array of enigmatic, narrative elements. Two disembodied arms hold a small dog around a woman’s shoulders in “The Milkman,” for instance, and a pensive woman walks by a display of numerous tiny vials in “Lachrymatories,” which in ancient Greece and Rome were used to hold perfumes but were once thought to collect mourners’ tears, earning them the name “tear bottles.”
“The Painter” (2026), pastel on paper, 9 7/8 x 8 1/4 inches
Through the use of pastels, Anstis retains “an intimate sense of touch that charges her scenes with introspective intensity,” the gallery says. The women in her works fully embody their surroundings, both emotionally and physically connecting to their activities, be it horseback riding, reading, or painting. Throughout, she evokes an air of veneration, as if to every scene there is some underlying rite or observance of which we’re only seeing a fragment. The artist tips her hat to the absurd, even the slightly cartoonish, tapping into the seductive irrationality of dreams and the imagination.
Pastels is on view through October 24 in New York City. See more on the artist’s Instagram.

“Tent” (2025), pastel on paper, 8 x 10 1/4 inches

title: A View From the Easel

Community

body:
Community
                “Sometimes it's infinite folding and binding, and I just spend the day or weekend doing that.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Welcome to the 354th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, printmaker and photographer Oswaldo García — whom I had the privilege of meeting at Pioneer Works's Press Play fair in 2024 — dances to cumbias while accordion-folding, book-binding, and watching the magical process of a printer churning out risographs.Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Oswaldo García, Columbia, MissouriHow long have you been working in this space?I moved from México and started an MFA two years ago at the University of Missouri-Columbia. I have been working in the Grad Studios building since then. I also work in the photolab studio and The Riso Room or Public House, depending if developing or printing.Describe an average day in your studio.I usually start working in the evening or at night sometimes (if going to book fairs). I'm teaching in the morning and taking classes. I work on everything at the same time — I collect, draft, research, make proofs, start thinking about new projects, print, fold, bind, and when I get tired of a project it helps me to move for some time to another. Then I go back and finish, but also sometimes it's infinite folding and binding, and I just spend the day or weekend doing that while listening to music. I dance and sing a lot while printing, especially cumbias, reggaetón, Mexican regional music, but a lot of pop, dance, everything. But if I'm drafting or thinking about a new project, I like the silence of my headphones.How does the space affect your work?I like the natural light, but I recently moved from my first studio to another one in the same building that has less of it, but I also like that for scanning and editing. This new studio has more space and that is helping me to expand the projects and let them breathe, to look at them differently and try arrangements and new compositions while working on many projects at the same time.How do you interact with the environment outside your studio?The building is all art studios and that motivates me to work. It's also nice to look at the process of others. I'm very inspired by people working in ceramics and fibers right now, and that has gotten me into trying those practices recently.What do you love about your studio?I love that it's like a blank canvas or paper that I can use to play and try assembling books, prints, projections, installations. And it is my safe space too, where I can always go and just be there with the work, materials, archive, books.What do you wish were different?I would love to have taller walls. I think I would go crazy doing bigger things! But I like how it is.

title: Brooklyn, Say Hello to Your First Craft Supply Library
description:
News
                Crochet hooks, thermal laminators, and button makers are among the 31 items now available to rent from the
body:
News
                Crochet hooks, thermal laminators, and button makers are among the 31 items now available to rent from the Brooklyn Public Library’s new lending program.
            
                
                                
                            
                
                
                    Anna Lee
                    September 11, 2026
                            — 2 min read
                    
                
            
        
            Materials for the linocut kit in the Brooklyn Public Library's new craft supply catalog (photo courtesy Brooklyn Public Library) The Brooklyn Public Library (BPL) officially launched its first-ever lending program for craft supplies on Wednesday, September 9. Crochet hooks, thermal laminators, and button makers are among the 31 items now available to rent from the BPL Craft Supply Library. The library consists of craft kits, such as linecut sets and woodworking apparatuses, which can be borrowed for three weeks, and craft tools, which can be borrowed for one week. Patrons with an adult library card can take up to three craft kits and two craft tools home at a time, at no charge, proving a welcome alternative for hobbyists who want to avoid hefty price tags. "All of us in New York are watching our budgets, and we have very limited storage," Fritzi Bodenheimer, a spokesperson for BPL, told Hyperallergic. "You can take something out from the library without that financial investment."The library’s holdings include a fourth-edition Cricut Maker, a nearly $400 machine that can cut, etch, and engrave into hundreds of materials.“Starting a new hobby or learning a new skill can mean a big investment in start-up tools or supplies, and often people don’t know if they’ll like the hobby,” Jessica Harwick, the BPL librarian behind the project, told Hyperallergic. “This collection will help remove that barrier so that more people can explore their creativity and try new things.”Wanting to merge her creative hobbies with her workplace, Harwick drew upon the pre-existing model for the BPL’s "Library of Things," which refers to all the library’s rentable materials that aren't books. David Bowie vinyls, culture passes to the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, and a Les Paul electric guitar are among the other items that can be rented for free with a public library card.As the craft library seeks to expand its collection, members of the public are encouraged to contribute gently used tools or supplies to the new project. While staff does not accept any "consumable" materials, such as yarn, paint, or glue, they review possible donations submitted to their dedicated email (craftsupplylibrary@bklynlibrary.org) on a case-by-case basis.The BPL launched the craft library to coincide with the ribbon cutting of the newly renovated Arts & Music space on the second floor of the Central Library on Grand Army Plaza. On top of functioning as the craft library's new home, the redesign by Toshiko Mori Architects houses a teen center and the new Eastern Parkway Collection Wing, which is stocked with art and music books. "It's really a part of a trend," Bodenheimer concluded. "A lot of people think a library is just books, but it's a lot more. The craft library is another part of that series."

title: Joel-Peter Witkin’s God-Loving, Gender-Bending Art
description:
Art Review
                His elaborate tableaux vivants blend elements of mythology, the Bible, and art history to express com
body:
Art Review
                His elaborate tableaux vivants blend elements of mythology, the Bible, and art history to express compassion for the marginalized.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Joel-Peter Witkin, "The Raft of George W. Bush" (2006) (photo David S. Rubin/Hyperallergic)LOS ANGELES — Although octogenarian Joel-Peter Witkin’s photography has sparked controversy for its sometimes macabre subject matter, his five-decade retrospective at Fahey/Klein Gallery reveals the practicing Catholic’s ongoing dedication to the principle that “we are all God’s children.” From the 1970s through 2018, when Witkin was diagnosed with dementia, he created tableau vivant photographs, using live models, props, and elaborate sets to create morality tales that blend elements of mythology, the Bible, and art history to express compassion for the marginalized, including people with dwarfism, amputees, and members of the LGBTQ+ community, especially those who are intersex.  Working exclusively with traditional cameras and black-and-white film, Witkin approaches each photo shoot like a director making a movie, building a set and developing his own prints. For expressive content, he often scratches a negative and treats an emerging print with bleach or encaustic, which can produce textural effects or color highlights. Joel-Peter Witkin, "Ecco Homo, NYC" (1975) (© Joel-Peter Witkin, image courtesy Fahey/Klein Gallery, Los Angeles)Witkin first explored gender bending in works such as “Ecce Homo, NYC” (1975), where a male hippie with sunglasses poses nude wearing high heels, his penis barely visible in dark shadows. The title equates him with art historical representations of Christ, while spotlighting his left foot on a draped table focuses on the female shoe and suggests that wearing it is a subversive act. A similar blend of dignity and edginess can be observed in multiple representations of intersex models, such as “The Three Graces, New Mexico” (1988), “Gods of Earth and Heaven, LA” (1988), which mimics Botticelli's “The Birth of Venus” (c. 1484–86), and “The Soul Has No Gender, Mexico” (2016), where a nude intersex person with long flowing hair is portrayed in radiant light holding a skull, in the tradition of memento mori portraiture. Three nails propped against the wall to the figure’s right suggest parallels between the persecution of Christ and the prejudicial abuses that people born with both male and female anatomy face today.The controversial “The Kiss (Le Braiser)” (1982) is among Witkin’s most metaphorically potent works. The subject appears to be two men smooching, yet it was actually constructed from a corpse’s head split in half, with one side turned around and pressed against the other. While symbolically affirming the legitimacy of same sex lovemaking, the imagery also conjures associations with narcissism and Witkin’s status as an identical twin (to another artist, the painter Jerome Witkin).

title: University of Michigan’s Fully Funded MFA Program Combines Studio Art and Research
description:
Announcement
                Top-ranked, tuition-free MFA program at University of Michigan's Stamps School of Art & Design supports
body:
Announcement
                Top-ranked, tuition-free MFA program at University of Michigan's Stamps School of Art & Design supports interdisciplinary, research-based practices  
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Crossways, Fiona Hoffer (MFA ’26), MFA Thesis Exhibition. Photo by Andy Maticorena Kajie
    
        
            The University of Michigan’s Penny W. Stamps School of Art & Design, ranked #11 nationally among graduate art and design schools by U.S. News and World Report, is now accepting MFA in Art applications for Fall 2027. The Stamps MFA brings students a uniquely supportive, critically engaged environment for interdisciplinary and research-based creative practice. Led by MFA Program Director Angela Washko, students develop materially sophisticated, conceptually rigorous work informed by funded travel and engagement with diverse communities, institutions, and creative contexts. Graduates emerge prepared to exhibit internationally, secure tenure-track positions at leading institutions, create public art, and shape cultural organizations worldwide.Throughout the two-year program, students engage with faculty from Stamps and tap into the boundless resources and collaborative opportunities that can only be found at the University of Michigan, TIME’s top public research university. Students also connect with nationally and internationally recognized visiting artists and critics through studio visits, critiques, and other events, gaining personalized feedback, fresh perspectives, and valuable professional connections.“I’ve been to a lot of MFA thesis shows around the country and I can say with confidence this is one of the best I’ve encountered — not only because of the strength and complexity and pleasures offered by the individual projects, but also because of the sense that the artists were talking and thinking together, learning and being inspired by each other. That such a strong sense of conversation could result in really unique and individual artistic voices is truly remarkable.”— Aruna D'Souza, Writer and Art CriticVisit the Stamps website to explore the Stamps MFA program through work from our most recent thesis exhibition, and to learn more about our graduate program in our upcoming events, including our Virtual Open House on Thursday, November 12, 2026.

title: 15 Fall Art -Ennials, From St. Louis to Dakar
description:
Guide
                A photography show dedicated to NYC in the nighttime, an Indigenous-led arts festival honoring the Mississ
body:
Guide
                A photography show dedicated to NYC in the nighttime, an Indigenous-led arts festival honoring the Mississippi River, the first-ever Bienal de Yucatán, and more biennials and triennials to visit across the world. 
                
        
            Adam Pape, "Amanda and the Night Picnic" (2018) (image courtesy the Museum of the City of New York)
    
        
            The 61st Venice Biennale is on view through late November, but fall is a time of beginnings, so it is only fitting that many other biennials and triennials opening across the world this season offer their own fresh starts. In a new triennial at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, design is wrested from its typical associations with materialism. A new biennial in Mérida in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula features 75 artists who work with the word and idiom in pursuit of new fabulations. The days may get shorter in autumn, but as evidenced at this year's photography edition of the Museum of the City of New York Triennial, the night shift proffers its own forms of vitality. Inspired by sci-fi author Ursula K. Le Guin's writings, the Converge 45 Triennial in Portland considers the new communities and discourses that form in the presence of art. Artists at the Toronto and Lyon Biennales work with migration, rupture, and extraction to not only transcribe tragic histories, but to chart speculative futures. And at this year's Alexandria Biennale, which returns to Egypt after a 12-year hiatus, we're reminded of the importance of resilience and protest amid today's global turmoil and permacrises, because This Too Shall Pass. — Phillip Pyle, associate editorWalker Design Triennial: Beyond MaterialismWalker Art Center, Minneapolis, MinnesotaOct. 17–Feb. 14, 2027Anna Aagaard Jensen, "Lady Chairs" (2018) (photo Iris Rijskamp, courtesy the artist and Walker Art Center)In the age of polyester, fast fashion, and TikTok Shop dupes, it’s difficult to remember that design exists for anything besides consumption. The inaugural Walker Design Triennial moves away from materialism and a post-industrial model of profit optimization, examining a recent shift towards spiritual cultivation in design. Across 95 works from an international array of artists and collectives, the exhibition examines how design can engage social issues, instead of exacerbating them. Bienal de Yucatán: VocalAcross various locations in Mérida, MexicoNov. 26–Feb. 28, 2027Yoko Ono, Teresa Margolles, Rirkrit Tiravanija, Oscar Murillo, and Jean-Luc Moulène are among the 75 artists participating in the inaugural Yucatán Biennial. Held in multiple venues across Mérida, a city known for its enduring Mayan heritage, the first edition of the exhibition is themed around language and idiom. International artists will work alongside local creators to explore how language traverses different territories, artistic processes, and disciplines. Museum of the City of New York Triennial: The Photography Triennial: After DarkMuseum of the City of New York, East Harlem, ManhattanNov. 20–April 25, 2027D'Angelo Lovell Williams, "Too Hot to Sleep (After Sylvester)" (2025) (courtesy the Museum of the City of New York)The second installment of MCNY's photography-centered triennial, which kicked off in 2023, this show will explore how New York City’s culture reaches new heights as the sky dims. Nightlife, the night shift, and the midnight munchies unfold in unison as the sun sets above the five boroughs, as documented by photographers including Elle Pérez, Tommy Kha, Saint Piñero, Dina Litovsky, Mahka Eslami, Liz Deschenes, D’Angelo Lovell Williams, and Kia LaBeija.Gwangju Biennale: You Must Change Your LifeGwangju Biennale Exhibition Hall, Gwangju, South KoreaThrough November 15“You must change your life” — the final line of Rainer Maria Rilke’s 1908 poem “Archaic Torso of Apollo” — is at once an open-ended declaration and a blunt call for transformation. Channeling that existential command through its title, the 16th Gwangju Biennale situates contemporary works, including deconstructed club rooms and webpage collages, in relation to art’s capacity to reflect change. 43 artists and groups explore change as an aesthetic phenomenon, a scalar metric, and a channel for transcending the self. Toronto Biennial of Art: Things Fall ApartAcross various locations in Toronto, CanadaSept. 26–Dec. 20Rebecca Belmore, "Flood" (2025) (courtesy Toronto Biennial of Art)Central to the Toronto Biennial’s fourth edition is the notion of rupture, namely through the avenues of migration and diaspora, waterways and borders, genocide and ecological justice, and speculative science fiction. Coco Fusco, Dawoud Bey, Kent Monkman, Skawennati, Dala Nasser, Wen Liu, and Simranpreet Anand are among the artists who look at disruption and its consequences as tools for transcribing history and unpacking the future.
